hints: Picture each halogen at room temperature and recall whether it is a gas, liquid or solid, then link each state to its characteristic colour.
walkthrough:
Visualise the three halogens at room temperature**
Think of what you would actually see in a lab bottle. Chlorine stays as a pale yellow-green gas, bromine is a fuming orange to brown liquid, and iodine is a shiny grey to black solid that gives a purple vapour on warming.
Final answer: Chlorine is a yellow-green gas, bromine is an orange to brown liquid, iodine is a grey to black solid.

hints: Remember that a stronger oxidising agent gains electrons more easily, and think about how electron gain changes as atoms get larger down Group 17.
walkthrough:
Link oxidising power to electron gain**
An oxidising agent oxidises another species by taking electrons from it, so it is itself reduced. Down Group 17 the atoms get larger and the incoming electron is attracted less strongly, so the ability to gain electrons and act as an oxidiser gets weaker from chlorine to bromine to iodine.
Final answer: Oxidising strength decreases from chlorine to iodine.

hints: Compare the colours of the reactants, chlorine and hydrogen, with the colour of the hydrogen chloride product.
walkthrough:
Track colour from reactants to product**
Chlorine is a yellow-green gas while hydrogen and hydrogen chloride are both colourless. When $\text{H}_2 + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}$ occurs, the only coloured species is used up, so you see the green colour disappear.
Final answer: The green colour disappears / is decolourised as colourless $\text{HCl}$ forms.

hints: Focus on the bond that must break when a hydrogen halide decomposes by heating, and how atomic size affects overlap and bond length down the group.
walkthrough:
Identify the bond controlling stability**
Thermal decomposition of $\text{HCl}$, $\text{HBr}$ and $\text{HI}$ requires breaking the $\text{H-X}$ covalent bond. A stronger bond needs more heat to break, so stability follows bond strength.

Explain why the bond weakens down the group**
Going from $\text{Cl}$ to $\text{I}$ the halogen atom gets much larger, so the $\text{H-X}$ bond gets longer with poorer orbital overlap. The bond is therefore weaker and breaks more easily, so thermal stability decreases.
Final answer: The $\text{H-X}$ covalent bond strength decreases down the group, so less thermal energy is needed to break it.

hints: Think about what makes homolytic fission different from heterolytic fission in terms of where the bonding electrons go.
walkthrough:
Picture an unpaired electron**
When a covalent bond breaks evenly, each atom keeps one electron from the pair. That leaves a highly reactive particle with a single, unpaired electron, often shown with a dot such as $\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$. That is a free radical.
Final answer: A species with one or more unpaired electrons.

hints: Recall what type of energy is needed to split $\text{Cl}_2$ into $\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$ radicals by homolysis at room temperature.
walkthrough:
Provide energy for homolysis**
Alkanes do not react with chlorine in the dark at room temperature because the strong $\text{Cl-Cl}$ bond needs energy to break evenly into radicals. Ultraviolet light supplies exactly that energy for initiation: $\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{uv} 2\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$.
Final answer: Ultraviolet light / sunlight.

hints: Remember that in propagation a radical reacts to make a new molecule plus a new radical, so the chain continues without net loss of radicals.
Start with $\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$ abstracting H from $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6$, then let the resulting carbon radical react with $\text{Cl}_2$ to regenerate $\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$.
walkthrough:
First propagation, make the alkyl radical**
A chlorine radical collides with ethane and removes a hydrogen atom. The $\text{C-H}$ bond breaks and $\text{H-Cl}$ forms, leaving an ethyl radical: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_6 + \text{Cl}^{\bullet} \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5^{\bullet} + \text{HCl}$$ One radical is used and a new carbon radical is created, so the chain continues.

Second propagation, make the product and regenerate the carrier**
The ethyl radical now attacks a chlorine molecule. It takes one chlorine atom to form chloroethane, releasing a fresh chlorine radical: $$\text{C}_2\text{H}_5^{\bullet} + \text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}^{\bullet}$$ That $\text{Cl}^{\bullet}$ can go back to Step 1, giving a continuous chain.

Final answer: $\mathrm{C_2H_6 + Cl^{\bullet} \rightarrow C_2H_5^{\bullet} + HCl}$
$\mathrm{C_2H_5^{\bullet} + Cl_2 \rightarrow C_2H_5Cl + Cl^{\bullet}}$

hints: Recall the two different reactions of chlorine with $\text{NaOH}$, and which temperature gives $\text{NaClO}$ rather than $\text{NaClO}_3$.
walkthrough:
Choose cold conditions for chlorate(I)**
Chlorine with alkali disproportionates. With cold, dilute sodium hydroxide you get sodium chlorate(I), the bleach ion: $$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Hot concentrated alkali would give $\text{NaClO}_3$ instead, so cold conditions are essential here.
Final answer: Cold dilute $\text{NaOH(aq)}$.

hints: Think about oxidation numbers and how the same element can both increase and decrease in oxidation number in one equation.
walkthrough:
Spot the same element going both ways**
In $\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, chlorine starts at 0. In $\text{NaCl}$ it is -1 (reduced, gained electrons) and in $\text{NaClO}$ it is +1 (oxidised, lost electrons). One starting species does both jobs at once, and that is disproportionation.
Final answer: A reaction in which the same species is both oxidised and reduced simultaneously.

hints: Count Cl, Na, C, H and O on each side and use the fact that three Cl atoms are needed to make $\text{CHCl}_3$ from $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3$.
walkthrough:
Balance by atom counting**
You need 3 Cl atoms to convert one $\text{CH}_3$ group into $\text{CHCl}_3$, so place 3 in front of $\text{NaClO}$. That gives 3 Na and 3 O on the left. On the right, one $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$ uses 1 Na and 2 O, leaving 2 Na and 1 O which fit exactly as $2\text{NaOH}$. Check H: left has 6, right has $1 + 3 + 2 = 6$. The balanced equation is: $$\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + 3\text{NaClO} \rightarrow \text{CHCl}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + 2\text{NaOH}$$
Final answer: $\mathrm{CH_3COCH_3 + 3NaClO \rightarrow CHCl_3 + CH_3COONa + 2NaOH}$

hints: Recall the normal observation when free chloride ions meet acidified silver nitrate solution.
Think about why $\text{CHCl}_3$ can still give that result even though its chlorine is covalent, by considering slow hydrolysis to release $\text{Cl}^-$.
walkthrough:
State the visible result**
Free $\text{Cl}^-$ with $\text{Ag}^+$ gives silver chloride, which is white. Here you also see a white precipitate, even though you started with covalent $\text{CHCl}_3$.

Explain where the ions come from**
In aqueous solution $\text{CHCl}_3$ slowly hydrolyses, breaking $\text{C-Cl}$ bonds and releasing chloride ions: $\text{Cl}^-$ then meets $\text{Ag}^+$ from $\text{AgNO}_3$ in the usual precipitation: $$\text{Ag}^+\text{(aq)} + \text{Cl}^-\text{(aq)} \rightarrow \text{AgCl(s)}$$ That is why the white solid appears.

Final answer: White precipitate forms.
$\text{CHCl}_3$ is hydrolysed to release $\text{Cl}^-$ ions which react with $\text{Ag}^+$ to form $\text{AgCl}$.
